standard questions when we want to tighten validation:
* does it prevent a no-op update of existing persisted objects that would fail this new validation? (would block storage migration tasks)
* does it prevent deletion of existing persisted objects with finalizers that would fail this new validation? (update is required to remove finalizers to allow deletion)
* does it prevent controllers from updating status of existing persisted objects that would fail this new validation?

we could consider ratcheting validation:
* apply this tightened validation on create
* apply this tightened validation on update where the old object passed this validation (don't let a valid object become invalid)
* skip this tightened validation on update where the old object fails this validation

c.f. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/59984

> it may render some API objects not valid, however, those objects are unusable by Kubernetes anyway, as it can't get the secrets with invalid names. Now the user gets an error earlier.

It would be good to note the places where an empty secret names produces a fatal error 100% of the time. Those are the only places we would consider tightening validation, but even there, we would not simply start marking the object as invalid... the validation would need to be aware of whether it was validating an update of an existing object that already contained empty secret name references, and tolerate the update in that case.

I wouldn't recommend refactoring existing validation AND adding tightening validation in the same PR... it makes it really hard to review to be sure we're not breaking compatibility.
I think Jordan is right in all points, this PR needs to be reworked to the ratcheting validation he suggests. Otherwise people won't be able to delete their newly invalid objects from the API server.

issue_context.title: The method of verifying the secret name is inconsistent, and the pvc/pv cannot be created normally
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:
1. I create a secret for pvc/pv, the name is: test.csi
2. create a pv with the secret test.csi as the bellow templates:  

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: test-csi-pv
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  csi:
    driver: disk.csi.everest.io
    fsType: ext4
    nodePublishSecretRef:
      name: test.csi
      namespace: default
    volumeAttributes:
      everest.io/disk-mode: SCSI
      everest.io/disk-volume-type: SATA
      storage.kubernetes.io/csiProvisionerIdentity: everest-csi-provisioner
    volumeHandle: 9bd54564-67a8-4827-a817-2243e53a81ad
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Delete
  storageClassName: csi-disk
  volumeMode: Filesystem
```
A failure error occurred, as bellow:  

```bash
# kubectl create -f testing-pv.yaml 
The PersistentVolume "test-csi-pv" is invalid: spec.csi.name: Invalid value: "test.csi": a DNS-1123 label must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters or '-', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (e.g. 'my-name',  or '123-abc', regex used for validation is '[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?')
```

#### What you expected to happen:

I reviewed the code [validateCSIPersistentVolumeSource](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L1538), and found: validate name with `ValidateDNS1123Label` .   
It's different with the `ValidateSecretName(apimachineryvalidation.NameIsDNSSubdomain)`. 

@jsafrane @sbezverk why not use the same way to validate Name in func `validateCSIPersistentVolumeSource`??   

Maybe use [ValidateSecretName](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L1589) is a good way.  


#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

1. create a secret, at least a dot in the secret name
2. create a pv, with the secret in nodePublishSecretRef items

#### Anything else we need to know?:

#### Environment:
- Any kubernetes version

review_comments:
I think I might be missing something here
As far as I understand, When we say SecretReference don't we mean both namespace and name, I mean if either of these is invalid then the secret itself is un-usable and thus the respective volume controller will not be able to use it anyway
cc @jsafrane

I agree a secret cannot be referred to if the name/namespace is missing from the secret reference, but the partial secret reference doesn't necessarily break the respective volume controller. 

The secret reference is an optional field in some PersistentVolumeSources. I think the first concern discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103024#issuecomment-874848298 was if a PersistentVolumeSource tolerates a partial secret reference (e.g. treats it as nil) and doesn't return a fatal error 100% of the time, then we cannot tighten the validation; otherwise we may break existing user workflow when we upgrade
Please add unit tests for this function.

In the [original issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102939#issuecomment-863050144), today people cannot write valid data because our validation is too tight. We should relax it.

Would you mind opening a new PR to change all the places that use `ValidateDNS1123Label` today into using `ValidateSecretName`?

Relaxing a validation is easier to reason about, and it addresses the original issue immediately.

This makes sense
I'll raise a PR with the change
Thank you for the review
